transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-21
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Lina Park (Redwood AE), Ravi Shah (Redwood SE), Ben Carter (Aequitas Infra), Maya Li (Aequitas ML), Tom Reynolds (Aequitas Security)
---
[00:00] Lina Park (Redwood AE): Hey everybody, thanks for joining. Want to do a quick agenda: 1) tradeoffs for where to run safety / moderation filters (inline vs sidecar vs pre-filter), 2) impact on latency and throughput, 3) KV cache and batching interactions, and 4) quantization/accuracy concerns and on-prem constraints. Ravi will lead the perf bits.
[00:22] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): cool. Ben, Maya, Tom, feel free to interrupt. Real quick, can you confirm your p95/p99 goals and whether you have a throughput estimate?
[00:35] Ben Carter (Infra): Our target is p99 <= 450ms for text-generation user flows, p95 around 120ms for short completions. Throughput: about 250 concurrent users peak, typical rate ~120 req/s. Those are soft numbers.
[00:52] Maya Li (ML): And for some evaluation endpoints we do long histories (2k tokens) so the KV/cache behavior matters a lot there.
[01:05] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Right. So first, filter placement. Three common patterns: 1) pre-filter client-side or edge (lightweight regex / heuristics), 2) inline safety layer inside the same inference process (synchronous), and 3) outboard async filter service (sidecar or separate model) that you can call either before or after generation, or as a streaming check.
[01:28] Tom Reynolds (Security): Quick Q: from a compliance perspective we need audit trails and deterministic block reasons; does outboarding lose fidelity?
[01:37] Lina Park (Redwood AE): Good point. We log filter decisions either way; outboarding actually helps because you can version and audit the filter model independently. But inline gives atomicity: a single request path either generates or is blocked.
[01:52] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Performance-wise, inline safety that runs in the same process as model execution can leverage token-level integration — e.g., compute filters on the same token stream as the model which reduces RPC overhead. But it increases per-token CPU and can affect batching. There's also memory pressure if the filter model needs KV or embeddings.
[02:18] Ben Carter (Infra): So inline sounds lower latency if co-located, but risks stability and scaling complexity?
[02:24] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Exactly. If the filter fails or spikes CPU, you can degrade the main serving pipeline. Outboard sidecar gives isolation: you can scale filters independently, put them on CPU-only nodes, or use a cheaper quantized model. But you pay extra network hop and added tail latency.
[02:43] Maya Li (ML): For our use-case, false negatives are bad; we prefer higher recall at cost of latency sometimes. But we do have a hard p99 target for UI flows.
[02:52] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Common pattern we've seen: edge pre-filter for obvious cases (deny words, phishing patterns), small fast heuristic to short-circuit; inline micro-checks for token-level streaming checks that must be immediate; and outboard heavy ML-based classifiers that run asynchronously or as a final gate. That combination balances throughput and quality.
[03:19] Lina Park (Redwood AE): Also mention of graceful degradation: if the sidecar times out, we can fallback to a safe default (e.g., mask content / return a generic blocked response) to preserve SLOs.
[03:32] Ben Carter (Infra): Can you quantify overhead? e.g., adding a sidecar model adds how much tail?
[03:38] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Ballpark: a simple CPU-based classifier call adds 8–40ms RPC per request depending on network and serialization. If you do token-level checks streaming, cost grows per-token, maybe 1–4ms/token extra. Inline deg can be 20–60ms per request if the filter runs synchronously before generation; but if integrated into the runtime as a lightweight op it can be much lower. The big hit is when the filter prevents batching — if you must run filter per-request before grouping, you lose batching benefits.
[04:10] Maya Li (ML): So batching is the dark horse. We rely on batching for cost — that reduces token cost substantially. How do filters affect batching?
[04:20] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Two ways: 1) pre-generation filters that must run before batch formation force per-request latency and block grouping. 2) post-generation checks allow generation to benefit from batching, but then you need a fallback if the output is disallowed. Post-checks can be async: allow generation to finish, mark content for review or do a fast policy rewrite. For strict flows you might reject generated content which causes user-visible failure.
[04:41] Ben Carter (Infra): Is there a hybrid: start generation optimistically, stream tokens to user but hold final commit until post-check passes?
[04:49] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Yes — optimistic streaming + confirm-on-final is a pattern. It increases complexity (need revocation, audit) but keeps latency good most of the time. The risk is exposing disallowed content during streaming.
[05:04] Tom Reynolds (Security): That's a dealbreaker for us — streaming exposing disallowed content even briefly is not acceptable.
[05:10] Lina Park (Redwood AE): That pushes toward in-path checks for user-facing flows, or at least edge blocking for high-risk prompts. We can still do optimistic for lower-risk internal tools.
[05:20] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Now KV cache and batching interplay: KV cache gives big speedups for long histories because subsequent requests reuse cached key/values. Safety filters that alter tokenization or canonicalization can reduce cache hits — e.g., if you normalize or add tokens for filters, cache indices shift. Also, if safety is inline and mutates generation (e.g., truncates or replaces), the KV cache needs to be coherent with the final output.
[05:52] Maya Li (ML): Our conversation histories are often user-specific and long, so loss of KV hit rate is a real cost. Any strategies?
[05:59] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Keep the safety checks orthogonal to model state: run filters on raw input text (pre-tokenize) and avoid injecting tokens into the generation path that would change KV keys. For runtime enforcement that needs to modify outputs, prefer post-processing (post-check + rewrite) instead of inserting tokens mid-run. Also, prefix caching strategies: maintain a separate cache namespace for canonicalized prompts to preserve hits.
[06:27] Ben Carter (Infra): How about quantization? We plan to use int8 or 4-bit on Dedicated GPUs to reduce cost. Does that affect safety model accuracy?
[06:36] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): It can. Quantization of the main model is often fine, but if you use small quantized safety models they may degrade recall slightly. We recommend testing the safety classifier across the same quantization profile. Sometimes you keep safety models in float16 on CPU/GPU while quantizing the generator. Or use a hybrid: generator in 4-bit, safety in 16-bit or an ensemble.
[06:56] Maya Li (ML): Any quick experiments we should run?
[07:00] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): We'll run a microbench where we measure: baseline gen p99 and throughput with batching and KV cache; then add inline filter in-process; then sidecar filter with async post-check; also run generator quantized vs float. We'll measure p50/p95/p99, token-cost, KV hit rate, and false positive/negative delta on your sample prompt set.
[07:22] Lina Park (Redwood AE): We'll share a bench template: a spreadsheet with columns for config, batch size, seq len, p50/p95/p99, kv_hit_rate, and false pos/neg. Link: https://redwood.example.com/bench-template (placeholder).
[07:36] Ben Carter (Infra): On-prem constraints: our on-prem infra has limited GPU mem per node; we may have to colocate filter on CPU-only hosts. How does Redwood accommodate that?
[07:47] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Redwood Private supports routing policies: you can pin filters to CPU nodes; the router will send inference traffic to nodes that maintain required co-location. If the filter is outboard, you can place it in the same VPC/subnet to keep latency low. For really constrained environments, we provide a lightweight C-wrapper binary that runs a simple heuristic filter locally and forwards ambiguous cases to a central sidecar. That's common in regulated deployments.
[08:14] Tom Reynolds (Security): KMS / key rotation concerns: do logs of filter decisions include any PII? We need to ensure policy logs don't leak PHI.
[08:24] Lina Park (Redwood AE): We support token-level redaction before logging and can route audit logs to your SIEM; we also integrate with customer-managed KMS for any encryption at rest. We'll include a SOC2/ISO note in the repo.
[08:37] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Back to perf: one non-obvious tradeoff is batching variance. When filters are synchronous pre-batch, you get very consistent small batches (bad for token cost). When filters are post-batch or async, you keep larger batch sizes but then need replay/fallback flows. There's also continuous batching: the runtime will batch requests opportunistically within a latency window (say 10–25ms). If pre-filtering extends that window or serializes requests, batching efficiency drops.
[09:10] Ben Carter (Infra): Any guidance for tuning batch windows and autoscaling with filters?
[09:17] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): For interactive UI flows where latency matters, use smaller max-batch windows (5–15ms) plus pre-filter heuristics to remove obviously blocked requests. For high-throughput back-office jobs, you can increase window to 50–200ms and push filters post-generation. Autoscaling: scale filter pool independently with CPU-based autoscaling rules based on queue depth; generator scales on GPU queue length.
[09:45] Maya Li (ML): You mentioned cache namespace. Can you expand?
[09:48] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Sure — keep a deterministic canonicalization step (e.g., normalize whitespace, lowercasing rules) and use that normalized prompt as a cache key. Make filter decisions based on original text but record canonical key mapping so you don't drop cache hits. You can also maintain multi-tier caches: hot prefix cache for long histories, and ephemeral per-session caches.
[10:12] Lina Park (Redwood AE): Let's talk numbers we saw in other customers: moving from pre-filter to post-filter increased batch size by ~2.5x and reduced per-token cost by ~38% in synthetic benchmarks; p99 increased by ~30–80ms depending on network. Inline filters reduced tail in some microbench because no network hops, but had higher variance when filter CPU spiked.
[10:36] Ben Carter (Infra): That cost delta matters. We'll need to balance cost vs the need for deterministic blocking.
[10:42] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Agreed. Our recommendation matrix: if regulators require blocking with no exposure, aim for inline or edge blocking. If you can tolerate delayed enforcement or post-hoc moderation, outboard yields better cost and throughput. For hybrid, run simple heuristics at the edge and heavy classification outboard.
[11:00] Maya Li (ML): Quick note on model ensembles: we might want an initial cheap classifier then a heavier ensemble if uncertain. Does Redwood support that routing?
[11:08] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Yes, routing policies support multi-stage pipelines. You can tag requests and route to different model tiers based on risk score. We also support function calls to orchestrate ensembles in the serving flow.
[11:20] Tom Reynolds (Security): From an audit perspective, keep every decision with model version and embedding of the reason; we need reproducibility.
[11:29] Lina Park (Redwood AE): We'll send our logging recommendations and a sample audit format.
[11:34] Ben Carter (Infra): What about fail-open vs fail-closed defaults during outages?
[11:38] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): That's policy-driven. Default in enterprise is fail-closed for high-risk flows — better to block than expose. But that affects availability; you need explicit SLA and fallback pages. We can help configure circuit-breakers and alerting.
[11:55] Maya Li (ML): Anything else on quantization? Edge cases like emotive or adversarial prompts?
[12:00] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Adversarial prompts can trip smaller quantized classifiers more. We recommend adversarial robustness tests in your bench. Also consider ensemble thresholds to reduce false negatives.
[12:12] Lina Park (Redwood AE): Let's summarize next steps.
[12:15] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): 1) Redwood runs KV-cache + batching benchmark across 4 configs (baseline, inline-filter, sidecar-post, sidecar-async) using your sample prompts. 2) Customer provides sample prompt set and SLOs. 3) Security will get the questionnaire. 4) We'll reconvene with results and a recommended placement plan.
[12:36] Ben Carter (Infra): That works. Can Ravi include expected infra reqs (CPU/memory) for sidecar filters?
[12:41] Ravi Shah (Redwood SE): Yes — I'll include typical CPU/RAM per classifier instance and expected p95 latency curves by batch size.
[12:49] Tom Reynolds (Security): Also include encryption notes and recommended redaction strategies.
[12:53] Lina Park (Redwood AE): We'll attach Redwood's security doc and the bench template.
[12:58] Maya Li (ML): Thanks — this was helpful.
[13:01] Lina Park (Redwood AE): Thanks all. We'll follow up with the spreadsheet and schedule a bench run.
